source_title: The 24 best slasher movies of all time, ranked - Entertainment Weekly
source_excerpt:
Like the unstoppable killers they depict, slasher is among the most enduring subgenres in horror. Though their cinematic origins are debatable, the groundwork was laid in 1960 with the release of two indelible horror classics : Alfred Hitchcock’s Psycho and Michael Powell’s Peeping Tom . These films helped establish a template that would evolve over time, spawning tropes including the final girl , the conflation of sex and death, and killers becoming franchise icons.
The slasher truly came into its own in the ‘70s, becoming increasingly relentless and gruesome before embracing camp in the ‘80s with a series of films featuring masked killers who stalked teens — the most successful of which launched iconic franchises . After the genre’s popularity waned, Wes Craven’s Scream (1996) revitalized the slasher with its self-referential approach, paving the way for a new wave of horror films in the late ‘90s.
Though the slasher has experienced its share of ups and downs, every once in a while a clever horror filmmaker comes along to revive and reinvigorate the genre with a splatterfest worthy of its predecessors. Below, Entertainment Weekly takes a stab at ranking the 24 best slasher movies of all time.
In 1979, a group of amateur actors and filmmakers rents a guesthouse on a remote Texas farm to shoot a low-budget porno. But when their bitter, sex-starved older hosts catch them in the act, their small production gets shut down as soon as the body count rises.
An homage to ’70s video nasties, Ti West ’s first installment of his X trilogy ranks among the chief slashers of the 2020s, putting a fresh spin on the genre with its sharp choices. While heavy on the carnage, this grindhouse-style horror goes beyond the guts and gore by delivering a masterclass in tension-building and weaving the themes of aging, beauty, and envy into a deeply unnerving tale. —James Mercadante
Molly (Jocelyn Jones) and her friends stumble upon Mr. Salusen (Chuck Connors) when their vehicle breaks down and he offers to help them. But things go from bad to worse when a mysterious masked man embarks on a killing spree.
Nearly 30 years after his first film role in Pat and Mike (1952), Connors agreed to be in Tourist Trap with the hope he’d introduce himself to a new generation of fans as a horror villain. But Connors didn’t become a scary movie maestro, and he constantly fought with Jones on set over their different approaches to the work: Connors taught himself the craft, and Jones practiced method acting. No, they didn’t get along. Check out EW’s interview with Dawn Jeffory-Nelson to find out how shooting Tina’s death scene “almost traumatized” the actress. —Steven Thrash
Where to watch Tourist Trap : Prime Video
He’s not Santa Claus, and there won’t be visions of sugar plums dancing in anyone’s head, but Billy (Robert Brian Wilson) is coming to town. Five-year-old Billy’s trauma comes from watching his parents being murdered by a man wearing Old Saint Nick’s wardrobe; as a young adult, Billy himself becomes a serial-killing Kris Kringle.
Silent Night, Deadly Night differs from other slashers in its juxtaposition of iconography. Seeing a Santa impostor commit heinous acts against the backdrop of powdery white snow and the glow of Christmas lights was jarring and mostly novel for the time, though 1974’s Black Christmas was, of course, ahead of that game. Still, the scandalous imagery is unforgettable, and it’s haunted audiences in a way most slasher films couldn’t. —S.T.
Where to watch Silent Night, Deadly Night : Prime Video
In the Canadian wilderness, some pesky teenagers unwittingly resurrect Johnny, a seemingly unstoppable masked killer who proceeds to stalk and murder them one by one. Unlike classic slashers, which would temporarily shift to the killer’s perspective, In a Violent Nature follows Johnny for most of its runtime. Indebted as much to Peeping Tom as it is to the ’80s era of the genre , the result is an experiential homage that’s light on dialogue and feels like watching ASMR for psychopaths.
Director Chris Nash doesn’t skimp on the gratuitous violence and gore, either, as Johnny dispatches those meddling kids using methods that were heretofore inconceivable. He basically invents new ways for people to die on screen. It’s disgusting, yes, but also wildly impressive. — Britt Hayes
Where to watch In a Violent Nature : Shudder
Much like Bill Murray does in the comedy classic Groundhog Day (1993), Tree (Jessica Rothe) relives the same day over and over again. And each time, she is killed by a mysterious assailant, leaving her no choice but to use the time loop to unravel the mystery of her murder before she succumbs to her repeated attacks.
Happy Death Day is a sterling representation of not only modern-day slashers, but the subgenre as a whole. Much of the film’s success is owed to its blending of horror and comedy, and Rothe herself described the picture as “ Groundhog Day meets Scream .” —S.T.
Where to watch Happy Death Day : Peacock
Ten-year-old Timmy (Alejandro Hernández) overreacts when his mother (May Heatherly) scorns him for playing with a jigsaw puzzle of a naked woman, prompting him to kill her with an ax and decapitate her with a hacksaw. 40 years later, Timmy (Edmund Purdom) lives a quiet life under his assumed identity (no spoilers here!), but his murderous appetite reignites when he witnesses a woman on a skateboard crash into a mirror.
The final scene is beyond shocking, and left unsuspecting audiences with one of the most cringe-worthy movie memories. Pieces is a worthy entry in the annals of horror history — and it happens to be Eli Roth’s favorite slasher film . —S.T.
Years after a traumatic boating accident, Angela (Felissa Rose) lives with her eccentric aunt Martha (Desiree Gould) and her cousin Ricky (Jonathan Tiersten). Martha sends the kids off to Camp Arawak for the summer, where their arrival coincides with the beginning of a serial killer’s violent spree.
Sleepaway Camp is a subversive spin on the Friday the 13th formula that’s delightfully weirder and more queer than its contemporaries. Notorious for its shocking twist ending and dismissed by critics upon its initial release, the film has since been reclaimed as a bona fide classic of the genre that still inspires fierce debate. — B.H.
Where to watch Sleepaway Camp : Prime Video
The prowler sports military fatigues and an advanced combat helmet, but he uses a pitchfork as his preferred instrument of death. After a couple is murdered in 1945, the elusive killer emerges 35 years later to wreak havoc again.
The film’s narrative structure plays out much like Friday the 13th as a horror/whodunit with the identity of the prowler remaining a secret until the end of the movie. The slasher later connected to the Friday the 13th franchise through its director, Joseph Zito, who would go on to helm one of the series’ best installments, Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter (1984). —S.T.
Where to watch The Prowler : Prime Video
A cruel prank goes awry when sorority girl Vicki (Eileen Davidson) shoots the house mother, Mrs. Slater (Lois Kelso Hunt). Rather than report the accident, Vicki and her sisters decide to hide the body and keep quiet. At the graduation party later that night, a killer emerges and begins to wipe out the women one by one. In Black Christmas style, the end of The House on Sorority Row is a classic slasher twist that leaves audiences wanting more.
The film cost approximately $450,000 to produce, and the investment paid off. The House on Sorority Row made $10.6 million domestically, and it remains one of the most memorable of the subgenre despite its formulaic approach. The movie even garnered a RiffTrax commentary from the former stars of Mystery Science Theater 3000 in 2018. —S.T.
Where to watch The House on Sorority Row : Prime Video
Six years after their 10-year-old sister Robin died in a tragic fall, Kim (Jamie Lee Curtis) and Robin’s fraternal twin brother Alex (Michael Tough) are getting ready for their high school prom. But a masked killer has plans for the big night, too: taking revenge on those responsible for Robin’s death.
Directed by Paul Lynch, Prom Night was developed in the wake of John Carpenter ’s Halloween — hence the Curtis casting — but distinguished itself with a more elaborate revenge story, conceived by Robert Guza Jr. and adapted for the screen by William Gray, complete with a classic third-act twist. — B.H.
Where to watch Prom Night : Prime Video
The Slumber Party Massacre starts from a familiar ‘80 premise: High-school senior Trish (Michele Michaels) decides to throw a slumber party while her parents are out of town. Unfortunately for Trish and her pals, a psycho killer wielding a power drill decides to crash the festivities.
Part of what makes The Slumber Party Massacre notable is that it was one of the few slasher films of the period directed by a woman — in this case, Amy Holden Jones. Though the screenplay was originally written by feminist author Rita Mae Brown as a parody of contemporary slashers, Jones’ more straightforward approach to the material makes for an unusual blend of horror and satire. — B.H.
Where to watch The Slumber Party Massacre : Prime Video
A fraternity prank goes too far when Alana ( Jamie Lee Curtis ) is coaxed into luring Kenny (Derek MacKinnon) into a sexual rendezvous, but instead of Alana, Kenny finds a corpse in the bed. Kenny is clearly traumatized, and, three years later, New Year’s Eve is anything but auld lang syne, as the same group of friends who tricked Kenny now find themselves targets of a vengeful killer.
The film is essentially Friday the 13th set on a train, but famed magician David Copperfield makes a cameo to set the movie apart from other slashers. Terror Train was the last of three horror films Curtis appeared in during 1980 alone, solidifying her reputation as a Scream Queen. —S.T.
Where to watch Terror Train : Screambox
Cropsy (Lou David) finds himself on the wrong end of a practical joke, and the camp caretaker is horribly burned. In I Know What You Did Last Summer style, the boys flee the scene rather than help him. Five years later, using a pair of garden shears, Cropsy takes his revenge on another summer camp.
The Burning marks the feature-film debuts of Jason Alexander, Holly Hunter, and Fisher Stevens. Meanwhile, special-effects horror icon Tom Savini (of many George Romero projects) actually turned down Friday the 13th Part 2 (1981) to work on The Burning instead. —S.T.
Where to watch The Burning : Prime Video
A group of friends gathers for spring break at Muffy’s (Deborah Foreman) island retreat, but the fun and games of April Fools’ pranks turn deadly when the teenagers fall prey to a mysterious killer — and the film’s ultimate prank remains one of the most underrated twists in horror history.
After working with Amy Steel on Friday the 13th Part 2 , producer Frank Mancuso Jr. recommended her for the role of Kit in April Fool’s Day five years later. On set, Mancuso noticed Steel enjoying the caterer’s fresh salmon, and he suggested she cut back on her lunches. Steel replied , “F--- you, no way,” as she should. —S.T.
Where to watch April Fool’s Day : Prime Video
Anthropology graduate student Helen Lyle’s (Virginia Madsen) research into local urban legends leads her to the Cabrini-Green public housing development in Chicago, where recent deaths have been attributed to Candyman ( Tony Todd ) — a vengeful spirit who wields a hook in place of a hand and is rumored to appear when his name is said five times in front of a mirror. Despite warnings from members of the local Black community, Helen continues pursuing the legend, only to find herself strangely drawn to Candyman and his tragic backstory.
Equal parts terrifying fable and supernatural slasher, and featuring a haunting score by Philip Glass, Bernard Rose’s film remains a singular horror classic. Perhaps Candyman ’s socially driven narrative concerning a white woman’s ill-advised investigation into a distinctly African-American horror story was ahead of its time. — B.H.
Where to watch Candyman : Prime Video
Abused by his sex-worker mother, Frank Zito (Joe Spinell) turns to a life of crime as an adult and becomes a vicious serial killer. Zito’s modus operandi is scalping women and attaching their hair to mannequins, which probably has nothing to do with his mommy issues...
Tom Savini truly works his magic in Maniac , and the special makeup effects are haunting, but the film also gets a boost from a pair of genre heavy-hitters. Spinell appeared in The Godfather and Rocky films, as well as Taxi Driver (1976), and Caroline Munro was well known as a Scream Queen, appearing in many horror films including The Abominable Dr. Phibes (1971), Dracula A.D. 1972 (1972), and Captain Kronos — Vampire Hunter (1974). —S.T.
A sorority is plagued by prank calls from a killer who targets them one by one. Jess (Olivia Hussey) and her friends must unravel the mystery of the distinctly voiced slayer — or no one will be able to celebrate Christmas this year.
Lois Lane herself, Margot Kidder, appeared in the film prior to her Superman days. Second City Television alumnus Andrea Martin also stars as one of the sorority sisters, and another famous comedian, Steve Martin, told Hussey he’d seen the movie 27 times. Director Bob Clark is not only the mastermind behind this slasher, but he also helmed another holiday classic, A Christmas Story (1983). —S.T.
Where to watch Black Christmas : Prime Video
Director Wes Craven and screenwriter Kevin Williamson created one of the most memorable slashers by deconstructing the very subgenre that made them both famous. Sidney (Neve Campbell) and her friends must abide by the rules of surviving a horror film to outlast the masked killer, Ghostface, in a metatextual genre ploy that essentially launched the ’90s teen screamer renaissance .
While housesitting for a friend, Williamson watched a television program about the “Gainesville Ripper.” The crimes of the real-life serial killer, Danny Rolling, didn’t have any bearing on Scream , but the eerie feeling Williamson experienced while watching the TV special reminded him of his favorite horror movie, Halloween (1978). That feeling, the phone call he had with a friend that night — and his dire financial straits — became the genesis of Scream , and horror is better for it. —S.T.
Psycho is often cited as the first slasher, but just as important to the genre is Peeping Tom . Released the same year as Hitchcock’s classic, Peeping Tom was directed by Michael Powell, a filmmaker best known for his masterful collaborations with Emeric Pressburger, including Black Narcissus (1947) and The Red Shoes (1948).
Powell’s 1960 film centers on Mark Lewis (Carl Boehm), a socially awkward aspiring filmmaker (something of a redundancy) who spends his days working on sets as a focus puller. In his off-hours, Lewis obsessively films himself murdering women, using a blade concealed in the tripod of his camera, then uses the footage to make his own personal snuff films. This unnervingly prescient exploration of voyeurism and cinematic obsession was controversial upon its release due to its depictions of sexuality and violence, but was later rightfully reappraised as a masterpiece with the help of Martin Scorsese . — B.H.
A group of teens traveling across rural Texas in a van stumbles upon the home of a family of murderous cannibals and their large adult son — a chainsaw-wielding maniac named Leatherface (Gunnar Hansen), who wears masks made from human skin.
From its haunting opening, featuring ominous narration by John Larroquette and grisly, documentary-style imagery, to its harrowing climax, The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is an exercise in relentless dread. Director Tobe Hooper makes the most of his limited budget, employing techniques that give the audience the impression that the film is much more gruesome than what is actually shown. But the film wouldn’t be nearly as effective without Marilyn Burns’ performance as Sally Hardesty, whose cathartic screams in the film’s final moments convey terror, relief, and a mind shattered by indescribable trauma — making The Texas Chain Saw Massacre a masterpiece. — B.H.
Where to watch The Texas Chain Saw Massacre : Prime Video
Death threatens the workers of a lowly summer camp on Crystal Lake, and it’s up to final girl Alice (Adrienne King) to stop the mysterious killer. Among the teenagers in peril are Kevin Bacon, who stars in only his fifth film project, and the son of legendary crooner Bing Crosby, Harry Crosby.
The real casting coup was choosing who played the killer, but the biggest twist comes in the final minutes of the film (no spoilers!) which has established enough lore to justify at least some of its sequels . Friday the 13th took Halloween ’s horror formula and improved on it by adding blood and gore — which became synonymous with the slasher genre moving forward. —S.T.
Where to watch Friday the 13th : Paramount+
A Nightmare on Elm Street spawned a franchise that became synonymous with Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund), the iconic dream-stalking killer with a penchant for delivering one-liners. But the first film, directed by horror master Wes Craven, is an effectively scary slasher that works well on its own (even if the increasingly campy sequels are entertaining as hell).
Teenager Nancy (Heather Langenkamp) and her friends begin having similar dreams about a disfigured man wielding a glove with razor-sharp blades attached to its fingers, only to learn the hard way that if he kills them in their sleep, they’ll die in real life. A Nightmare on Elm Street was revelatory in 1984, thanks in large part to its original villain (and Englund’s excellent performance), as well as Craven’s use of special effects and set design to show his characters being thrashed around violently in their sleep as Freddy slaughters them in their dreams. — B.H.
Where to watch A Nightmare on Elm Street : HBO Max
Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) sits with the clerk of the Bates Motel, Norman (Anthony Perkins). Their conversation seems pleasant enough until she suggests putting Norman’s overbearing mother in an asylum. Later in Marion’s hotel room, as she takes a shower, Mrs. Bates takes her revenge in what’s still one of the most iconic scenes in the history of film.
It isn’t 40 whacks like Lizzie Borden, but director Alfred Hitchcock still violently kills off his leading lady in the opening reel of the must-see slasher. Psycho was Hitchcock’s first horror flick, and the picture included a William Castle-style gimmick: Theater managers were ordered not to admit anyone who arrived late , not even the Queen of England. —S.T.

After slaying his sister as a young boy, now-adult Michael Myers escapes from Smith’s Grove Sanitarium and returns to his hometown of Haddonfield, where he takes a disturbing interest in Laurie Strode (Jamie Lee Curtis) and her high school friends. Myers’ doctor, Sam Loomis (Donald Pleasence), pursues the speechless killer, but even he can’t stop the carnage.
These days, it might be hard to believe that Halloween was produced for just $300,000 . The investment in director John Carpenter paid off, and the movie grossed more than $47 million domestically, making it the highest-grossing independent movie for years. Unlike the slashers to follow, Halloween relies on suspense rather than blood and gore to scare audiences, a technique that still cements it as the greatest slasher film of all time. —S.T.
